title: The Fall
hook: In Moses 5:11, after being expelled from Eden, Adam offers sacrifice without understanding why—until an angel appears and declares, 'This thing is a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten of the Son.' Adam had been performing temple ordinances for years before receiving their meaning. This stunning detail, restored through Joseph Smith, reframes the entire narrative of the Fall: Adam and Eve didn't stumble into mortality—they chose it deliberately, then immediately began temple worship that pointed toward Christ's Atonement. The Fall wasn't humanity's tragic mistake; it was the essential first step in God's plan of salvation. This week's chapters invite us to see Eden not as paradise lost, but as mortality courageously gained.
overview:
Genesis 3–4 and Moses 4–5 present the same foundational narrative through different lenses—the King James translation and Joseph Smith's inspired expansion. The account begins with the serpent's approach to Eve in the Garden, her choice to partake of the forbidden fruit, Adam's deliberate decision to join her, and their subsequent expulsion from Eden into a world of toil, thorns, and mortality. Genesis 4 and Moses 5 then chronicle the first generation born outside Eden: Cain and Abel's offerings, Cain's murder of his brother, and the beginning of two distinct lineages—those who call upon the name of the Lord and those who love Satan more than God. The narrative arc moves from innocence through choice into the full complexity of mortal existence, establishing patterns that will echo through all of scripture.

The central theological contribution of these chapters is the doctrine of the fortunate Fall—the understanding that Adam and Eve's transgression was not sin in the traditional sense but a necessary stepping-down into mortality that made eternal progression possible. Moses 5:10-11 preserves Eve's stunning declaration: 'Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed, and never should have known good and evil, and the joy of our redemption.' This transforms the Christian reading of Genesis entirely: the Fall becomes an act of informed agency, not naive disobedience. Lehi will later teach that 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy' (2 Nephi 2:25), placing joy—not merely probation—at the center of mortal existence. The Book of Mormon and the Pearl of Great Price rescue the Fall from Augustine's doctrine of original sin and restore it as the hinge upon which God's entire plan turns.

Linguistically, the Hebrew wordplay in Genesis 3 is theologically rich. The word for 'subtil' (arum) describing the serpent in Genesis 3:1 is a pun on 'naked' (arummim) in Genesis 2:25—Adam and Eve were 'naked and not ashamed,' while the serpent was 'more subtle than any beast.' After eating, 'the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked' (Genesis 3:7)—the same word returns, but now clothed in shame. The garments of skins God provides in Genesis 3:21 (Hebrew: kotnot or, 'tunics of skin') become in ancient Jewish tradition 'garments of light' (kotnot or), suggesting something more than animal hides—a reading that resonates deeply with Latter-day Saint temple understanding. Moses 4:13 adds the crucial detail that Satan 'knew not the mind of God, wherefore he sought to destroy the world'—establishing that the adversary's designs are rooted in ignorance, not merely malice.

The Joseph Smith Translation makes critical additions throughout these chapters. In Moses 4:6-12, we learn that Satan 'sought also to beguile Eve, for he knew not the mind of God.' The JST clarifies that the commandment not to partake was given with a contingency: 'Nevertheless, thou mayest choose for thyself' (Moses 3:17)—agency was built into the restriction from the beginning. Moses 5 adds entire narratives absent from Genesis: Adam and Eve's continued revelations, the clarity that they taught their children 'all things concerning the plan of redemption,' and Cain's explicit covenant with Satan. These restorations don't merely supplement Genesis; they fundamentally alter its meaning, revealing a premortal plan, a Christ-centered sacrifice system, and generations who had the gospel taught to them with clarity.

Every element of the Fall narrative points toward Christ. The coats of skins require the death of animals—the first death in Eden is to cover the consequences of the Fall, prefiguring the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. Adam's sacrifices in Moses 5:5-7 are 'a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten,' and an angel teaches him the purpose: 'Thou shalt do all that thou doest in the name of the Son, and thou shalt repent and call upon God in the name of the Son forevermore.' The protevangelium in Genesis 3:15—the promise that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head—is Christianity's first messianic prophecy, delivered in the moment of judgment. Cain's rejection of the required sacrifice parallels every covenant breaker who seeks salvation on his own terms. The entire narrative establishes that mortality is both consequence and gift, and redemption through Christ was the plan before the foundation of the world.

key_verses.text_kjv: And Eve, his wife, heard all these things and was glad, saying: Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed, and never should have known good and evil, and the joy of our redemption, and the eternal life which God giveth unto all the obedient.
key_verses.insight: Eve is the first theologian, articulating the doctrine of the fortunate Fall with stunning clarity. Her response is not shame but gladness, recognizing that the transgression made possible not just mortality but 'the joy of our redemption.' This verse reframes the entire Eden narrative—Eve understands what happened better than most Christians throughout history.

key_verses.text_kjv: And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
key_verses.insight: The protevangelium—the 'first gospel'—promised in the moment of judgment. The seed of the woman (Christ, born of Mary) will crush the serpent's head, though suffering a heel wound in the process (the crucifixion). This prophecy establishes from Genesis 3 that a Redeemer was always part of the plan, not an emergency response to the Fall.

key_verses.text_kjv: And after many days an angel of the Lord appeared unto Adam, saying: Why dost thou offer sacrifices unto the Lord? And Adam said unto him: I know not, save the Lord commanded me. And then the angel spake, saying: This thing is a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten of the Father.
key_verses.insight: Adam performs temple ordinances for perhaps years before understanding their meaning—an echo of every covenant member who participates in ordinances that unfold their significance over a lifetime. The angel's explanation makes explicit what Genesis only implies: worship from Eden forward was Christocentric, pointing toward the Atonement.

key_verses.text_kjv: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it became pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make her wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and also gave unto her husband with her, and he did eat.
key_verses.insight: The JST preserves the detail 'with her'—Adam was present during Eve's conversation with the serpent, not absent as popular retellings often suggest. This detail eliminates the narrative of Eve as lone deceiver and Adam as passive victim, restoring them as partners who together stepped into mortality.

key_verses.text_kjv: And Adam and Eve blessed the name of God, and they made all things known unto their sons and their daughters.
key_verses.insight: The first family held scripture study. Adam and Eve taught their children 'all things concerning the plan of redemption' (Moses 5:12). Cain's rebellion was not ignorance but willful rejection of revealed truth. This establishes a pattern: apostasy happens not in the absence of truth but in its presence, when individuals choose another way.

highlights.snippet_text: Moses 4 opens with the premortal council entirely absent from Genesis—Lucifer's offer to 'redeem all mankind, that one soul shall not be lost,' and his demand for God's honor in return. This JST restoration reveals that Satan's plan wasn't obviously evil; it was safety without agency, salvation without choice. The Fall makes sense only against the backdrop of this premortal debate about freedom.
highlights.label: Restoration

highlights.snippet_text: Adam names his wife 'Eve' (Hebrew: Chavah) because she is 'the mother of all living.' The Hebrew root chavah means 'to live' or 'to give life.' In a world newly introduced to death, Adam's first act is to name his partner after life itself—a profound theological statement about her role and identity, and a rejection of death as the final word.
highlights.label: Hebrew

highlights.snippet_text: God warns Cain, 'sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.' The phrase 'lieth at the door' uses the Hebrew word robets, a predatory animal crouching to pounce. Paul later echoes this imagery in Romans 6:12-14, urging believers not to let sin 'reign' in their mortal bodies. Sin is personified as a beast we must master or be devoured by.
highlights.label: Cross-Ref

highlights.snippet_text: Moses 5:29-31 introduces the covenant Cain makes with Satan: 'Swear unto me by thy throat... that thou wilt not tell it.' This is the origin of secret combinations, later elaborated in the Book of Mormon (Helaman 6:26-30). The Restoration reveals that organized evil through secret oaths began with Cain and has plagued every dispensation since.
highlights.label: Restoration

highlights.snippet_text: God tells Eve, 'thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.' Elder Dallin H. Oaks taught this describes a consequence of the Fall, not a commandment: unrighteous dominion is a broken pattern to overcome, not a divinely mandated hierarchy. The plan of salvation lifts marriage toward partnership, not rulership.
highlights.label: Prophetic

highlights.snippet_text: After leaving Eden, 'Adam and Eve... called upon the name of the Lord.' Prayer becomes the first act of mortal life outside paradise. When we lose our place of spiritual security—whether through sin, tragedy, or transition—calling upon God is the pattern established by our first parents. We pray our way into understanding, not the reverse.
highlights.label: Application

restoration_lens:
The Restoration's most profound contribution to the Fall narrative is the recovery of its purposefulness. Joseph Smith's revelations—particularly the Book of Moses and the Book of Mormon teachings on the Fall—rescue Adam and Eve from centuries of Christian misreading that cast them as tragic failures whose sin cursed all humanity. Instead, Restoration scripture reveals that the Fall was anticipated, necessary, and ultimately fortunate. The premortal council scene in Moses 4:1-4 establishes that two plans were presented: Lucifer's guarantee of universal salvation without agency, and the Father's plan that required a fall into mortality, probation through opposition, and redemption through the sacrifice of His Son. The Fall was not Plan B; it was always the means by which God's children would become like Him. Lehi teaches in 2 Nephi 2:22-25 that without the Fall, Adam and Eve 'would have remained in a state of innocence, having no joy, for they knew no misery; doing no good, for they knew no sin.' Innocence is not exaltation—it is stasis. The Fall initiated the dynamic process of becoming.

The Joseph Smith Translation adds critical clarifications throughout Genesis 3. Moses 3:17 preserves that the commandment not to eat included the phrase 'Nevertheless, thou mayest choose for thyself, for it is given unto thee'—agency was embedded in the restriction from the beginning, not violated by the choice. Moses 4:11 clarifies that Satan 'knew not the mind of God, wherefore he sought to destroy the world'—the adversary's designs are rooted in misunderstanding God's purposes, not simply in rebellion. Moses 5 expands the Genesis 4 account dramatically, adding that Adam and Eve 'made all things known unto their sons and their daughters' regarding the plan of redemption (Moses 5:12), that an angel taught Adam the meaning of sacrifice as 'a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten' (Moses 5:7), and that Cain made an explicit covenant with Satan (Moses 5:29-31), becoming 'Master Mahan' and the father of secret combinations. These additions transform a sparse narrative into a robust theological foundation: the first family had temple worship, a revealed plan of salvation, and a clear choice between covenant faithfulness and rebellion.

The temple connections in these chapters are profound and intentional, though appropriately subtle in public scripture. The pattern of instruction, covenant, and garments in Genesis 3 resonates with the endowment structure. Adam and Eve receive commandments, are taught by heavenly messengers, make choices with eternal consequences, and are clothed by God Himself before being sent into the world. Moses 5 establishes that sacrifice—the central temple ordinance until the crucifixion—was instituted immediately after the Fall and was explicitly identified as pointing toward Christ's Atonement. The Book of Abraham further reveals that these temple teachings were part of the premortal plan: 'We will prove them herewith, to see if they will do all things whatsoever the Lord their God shall command them' (Abraham 3:25). President Russell M. Nelson has taught that temple covenants connect us to 'the same spiritual pattern that Adam and Eve and their posterity have followed.' The narrative of the Fall is not ancient history; it is the template for every individual's covenant journey from innocence through choice into redemption.
application:
For modern covenant members, the doctrine of the fortunate Fall is liberating and demanding in equal measure. Liberating because it reframes our mortal struggles—the toil, the opposition, the disappointments—not as evidence that something has gone wrong, but as the very conditions necessary for growth. Eve's declaration that the Fall made possible 'the joy of our redemption' (Moses 5:11) means that difficulty is not the absence of God's blessing but often its purest form. Parents navigating the chaos of raising children in a fallen world can take courage from knowing that Adam and Eve's first act after Eden was to teach their children the plan of salvation—they didn't wait for perfect conditions or complete understanding. Returned missionaries wrestling with a world that doesn't resemble the clarity of the mission field can recognize that the pattern of Adam offering sacrifice for years without understanding why (Moses 5:6) is normal, not faithless. We covenant our way into understanding, not the reverse. The application of these chapters is the long view: mortality is not a problem to be solved quickly but a laboratory in which eternal beings are refined.

The narrative of Cain and Abel speaks directly to the dangers of comparing our offerings to others' and defining our worship by our own preferences rather than God's revealed will. Moses 5:18-23 clarifies that Cain's offering was rejected not arbitrarily but because he 'loved Satan more than God' and 'offered not the firstlings of his flock.' He brought what was convenient, not what was required. This challenges every covenant member who wants to negotiate with God about the terms of discipleship—whether it's questions about tithing on net versus gross, about Sabbath observance that accommodates personal preference, or about temple attendance when 'busy seasons' become permanent. The standard is not sincerity alone but obedient sacrifice. Simultaneously, the Lord's question to Cain in Genesis 4:6-7—'Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted?'—reveals God's patient invitation even to those who rebel. The door to repentance remained open to Cain until the moment he murdered Abel. For those struggling with faith, resentment, or spiritual apathy, the lesson is clear: repentance is available now, but the trajectory of small compromises leads to hard-heartedness.

Perhaps the most challenging application is the call to recognize that we are all, like Adam and Eve, participants in an ongoing Fall and redemption. We leave our own spiritual Edens—seasons of innocence, clarity, or closeness to God—through choices both necessary and unwise. The question is whether we respond like Adam and Eve—who called upon God, offered sacrifice, taught their children, and blessed His name despite exile—or like Cain, who resented the terms of redemption and ultimately sought his own glory. President Dallin H. Oaks taught, 'The Fall was not a disaster. It was a deliberate plan... We celebrate the Fall and the opportunity it offers for growth.' That celebration is not theoretical; it happens when a struggling parent prays after a hard day, when a temple-goer returns week after week without immediate answers, when a covenant member chooses obedience over convenience. The application of Genesis 3–4 and Moses 4–5 is the daily choice to trust that God's plan is greater than our comfort, and His timeline is longer than our mortality.
